::: {.column style="width: 50%; align-self: center;"}
- Models help us understand the behaviour of populations over time.
- **Declining populations** of particular interest.
- **Simulation** lets us test, validate, and calibrate inference methods.
- Necessary for **statistical methods** (bootstrap) or **training models** (machine learning).
:::
::::

::: notes
I hardly need to be telling this audience,
but models help us understand how populations behave, and let us ask counter-factuals.

One motivating factor might be to study Declining populations
Frog: Vulnerable
Parrot: Critically Endangered - got down to 14 birds in Feb 2017

- want to simulate long trajectories, non-extinct
:::

## Subcritical birth-and-death processes can model declining populations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![](figures/bdp_tree_2.svg){width="720"}
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
- Birth-and-death process: per individual **birth-rate** $\lambda$, **death-rate** $\mu$.
- **Subcritical** if $\mu > \lambda$.
- Observe **non-extinct** processes at finite time $T$.
- How to simulate **conditioned on survival**?
:::
::::

::: notes
- Over time we expect that that the population would decrease
- Tree representation, time y axis
- Observe the process at some finite time $T$ after the process has started.
:::

## Naive simulation becomes increasingly costly for longer times and more subcritical processes

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.algo}
**Naive (Doob--Gillespie) simulation**

1. $t \leftarrow 0$, $n \leftarrow 1$
2. **while** $t < T$ and $n > 0$:
    - draw $\Delta \sim \mathrm{Exp}\big(n(\lambda+\mu)\big)$ and set $t \leftarrow t + \Delta$
    - birth ($n \leftarrow n+1$) with probability $\frac{\lambda}{\lambda+\mu}$, otherwise death ($n \leftarrow n-1$)
    - assign the birth/death uniformly at random to the individuals in the process.
3. **if** $n = 0$: discard and restart; **else** keep the tree
:::
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
- For $\mu > \lambda$: $\Pr(\text{Non-Extinct})$ grows exponentially small with $T$
- Runs needed per survivor: $1 / \Pr(\text{Non-Extinct})$
- $\lambda = 1$, $\mu = 2$, $T = 10$: about **44,000** runs
:::
::::

::: notes
- The probability of survival decreases exponentially with time.
- The number of runs needed increases dramatically as the process becomes more subcritical.
- Does give exact independent simulations
:::

## Multilevel splitting is more efficient at simulating subcritical processes, but yields correlated trees

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
::: {.algo}
**Modified multilevel splitting**

Given levels $0=\tau_0 < \tau_1 < \dots < \tau_J = T$, cloning rates $r_j$ and size $N_0$.

1. Start $N_0$ processes from the initial distribution
2. **for** $j = 1, \dots, J$:
    - run each process using Doob--Gillespie to level $\tau_j$
    - discard those that did not reach $\tau_j$
    - clone each survivor $r_j$ times
3. **return** trees that survived to $T$ (if any)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}
- Made for **unbiased estimators** of rare-event probabilities:
$$\hat{p} = \frac{\text{\# surviving trees}}{N_0 \prod_{j=1}^{J} r_j},$$
and
$$\mathbb{E}\bigl(\hat p\bigr) = \Pr(Z_T > 0)$$
- Set of trees **highly correlated** (shared ancestry)
:::
::::

::: notes
- draw levels and tree on blackboard
:::

::: {.refs}
Glasserman, Heidelberger, Shahabuddin & Zajic (1999). Multilevel splitting for estimating rare event probabilities. *Operations Research* 47(4), 585--600. [doi:10.1287/opre.47.4.585](https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.47.4.585)

Braunsteins, Hautphenne & Minuesa (2022). Parameter estimation in branching processes with almost sure extinction. *Bernoulli* 28(1), 33--63. [doi:10.3150/21-BEJ1332](https://doi.org/10.3150/21-BEJ1332)
:::

## A tree is encoded by its contour

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
![](figures/tree_contour_1.svg){width="740"}

![](figures/tree_contour_2.svg){.fragment fragment-index=1 width="740"}
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}

- Explore the tree **depth-first**, height over time: the **contour**.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- Peaks: **deaths** (or $T$), valleys: **births**.
- Can we simulate the contour **directly**?
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
- Instead of looking at a trees, we are going to consider a related quantity, which is their contour.
- Explore at constant rate.
- Importantly there is a one-to-one mapping between trees and their contours,
and so what that basically means is, if I give you a DFS/contour,
you can reconstruct the tree it was searching.
:::

## A contour is a simple Markov chain of extrema

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](figures/tree_contour_3.svg){width="740"}
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
- The extrema form **Markov chain**:
    - **up** by $\mathrm{Exp}(\mu)$
    - **down** by $\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$.
- Truncate at $T$, stop on hitting $0$.
- Extrema $\mapsto$ Contour $\mapsto$ Tree.
:::
::::

::: notes
Each contour can be unique characterised by its extrema,
since the contour itself is just a linear interpolation between the extrema.

The reason for steps up with rate mu is that up jumps correspond to lifetimes,
and down jumps correspond to births, which occur at rate lambda.

So now the problem becomes simulating a Markov chain of extrema, conditioned on hitting T before 0.
:::

## Only the first ascent of a contour is hard

::: {.r-stack}

![](figures/tree_contour_5.svg){width="900"}

![](figures/tree_contour_4.svg){.fragment fragment-index=1 width="900"}

![](figures/tree_contour_5.svg){.fragment fragment-index=2 width="900"}
:::

::: notes
The way we can think about it is as follows:

- We need a first ascent to reach T (next slide)
- and then we need a descent to reach 0 (next slide)
- this descent is easy to simulate, because starting at T,
the chain has a downward drift **in a sub-critical regime**, and so is drawn to 0. (next slide)
- the hard part is still this first ascent, because starting at 0, the chain has an upward drift, and so is drawn to T.
- the key idea here will be to try and also simulate this first ascent,
but backwards in time relative to the depth-first search.
:::

## Parent--child relationships can be exchanged

::::: {.columns style="align-items: center;"}
::: {.column style="width: 50%; align-self: center;"}
![](figures/birth_exchange_1.svg){.nostretch fig-alt="An unlabelled tree" style="width: 100%; height: auto; max-height: none; max-width: 100%; margin: 0;"}
:::

::: {.column style="width: 50%; align-self: center;"}
![](figures/birth_exchange_2.svg){.nostretch .fragment fig-alt="The tree and its birth-exchanged tree, linked by the birth exchange" style="height: 540px; width: auto; max-height: none; max-width: 100%; margin: 0;"}
:::
:::::

::: notes
- The key to this little trick is understanding the relationship between contours
in trees where you exchange the parent-child relationships at each birth.
- Forget which branch at each birth is the mother and which the daughter: the unlabelled tree.
- Every labelling is equally likely (next slide)
- So we can consider labelling the left individual as the mother and the right individual as the daughter, or vice versa, and the contours will be the same, but reversed in time.
:::

## The hard ascent is a reversed easy descent

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
![](figures/exchanged_pair_1.svg){width="690"}

![](figures/exchanged_pair_2.svg){.fragment fragment-index=1 width="690"}
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}

- Exchanging all parent-child relationships: the contour is **reversed**.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
- First ascent = **reversed** last descent.
- So **simulate a descent** and reverse it.
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
First ascent has the same distribution as the last descent reversed in time, and so we can simulate a descent and reverse it to get the first ascent.
Last descent just ignore first times it hits T, explain this is why get more efficient as more subcritical.
:::

```{python}
#| include: false
import importlib.util
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import altair as alt
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown, display


def load(name: str, path: Path):
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location(name, path)
    module = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    sys.modules[name] = module
    spec.loader.exec_module(module)
    return module


def find_root() -> Path:
    here = Path.cwd().resolve()
    for candidate in (here, *here.parents):
        if (candidate / "scripts" / "bench_method_comparison.py").exists():
            return candidate
    msg = "Run from inside the bdsurv repository."
    raise FileNotFoundError(msg)


ROOT = find_root()
PARAM_STYLE = "font-size: 0.72em; color: #4a6670;"
bench = load("bench_method_comparison", ROOT / "scripts" / "bench_method_comparison.py")
charts = load(
    "method_comparison_charts", ROOT / "scripts" / "method_comparison_charts.py"
)
```

## The more subcritical, the bigger the speed-up

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{python}
T_DRAWS = 60.0
draws = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "benchmarks" / "data" / "draws.csv")
draws = draws[(draws["model"] == "constant") & (draws["T"] == T_DRAWS)]
draw_curves = charts.curves_from_draws(draws)
draw_mus = sorted(draw_curves["mu"].unique())

draw_linear_x = charts.cost_chart(
    draw_curves,
    alt.X(
        "mu:Q",
        scale=alt.Scale(domain=[min(draw_mus), max(draw_mus)], nice=False),
        title="death rate μ",
        axis=alt.Axis(values=[1, 5, 10, 15, 20], format="g"),
    ),
    lam=bench.LAMBDA,
    statistic="mean",
    measure="draws",
    mark_critical=True,
    legend_font_size=21,
    width=960,
    height=265,
)

draw_mean = draw_curves.pivot_table(index="mu", columns="method", values="mean")
draw_top = max(draw_mus)
draw_ratio = (
    draw_mean.loc[draw_top, charts.LABEL_RUN]
    / draw_mean.loc[draw_top, charts.LABEL_CONTOUR]
)
display(
    draw_linear_x.configure(font="Libertinus Serif", background="#FAFAFA")
    .configure_axis(labelFontSize=22, titleFontSize=26)
    .configure_legend(symbolSize=200)
)
display(
    Markdown(
        f"At $\\mu = {draw_top:g}$, splitting draws "
        f"**{draw_ratio:,.0f}×** more random numbers.\n\n"
        f'[$\\lambda = {bench.LAMBDA:g}$, $T = {T_DRAWS:g}$]{{style="{PARAM_STYLE}"}}'
    )
)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in fragment-index=1}
```{python}
T_SHOWN = 60.0
rows = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "benchmarks" / "data" / bench.ROWS_FILE)
curves = charts.curves_from_rows(rows)
at_t = curves[curves["T"] == T_SHOWN]
mus = sorted(at_t["mu"].unique())

chart = charts.cost_chart(
    at_t,
    charts.x_by_mu(mus),
    lam=bench.LAMBDA,
    statistic="mean",
    mark_critical=True,
    legend_font_size=21,
    width=960,
    height=265,
)
display(
    chart.configure(font="Libertinus Serif", background="#FAFAFA")
    .configure_axis(labelFontSize=22, titleFontSize=26)
    .configure_legend(symbolSize=200)
)

mean = at_t.pivot_table(index="mu", columns="method", values="mean")
mu_top = max(mus)
speedup = mean.loc[mu_top, charts.LABEL_RUN] / mean.loc[mu_top, charts.LABEL_CONTOUR]
display(
    Markdown(
        f"Time per tree: at $\\mu = {mu_top:g}$, splitting "
        f"costs **{speedup:,.0f}×** more.\n\n"
        f'[$\\lambda = {bench.LAMBDA:g}$, $T = {T_SHOWN:g}$]{{style="{PARAM_STYLE}"}}'
    )
)
```
:::

## What if the birth and death rates vary?

- Birth rate $\lambda(t)$ and death rate $\mu(t)$ change with time.

::: notes
- So far the rates were constant.
- Next: the simplest case where the death rate grows with time.
:::

## An Arley process: the death rate grows with time

```{python}
acharts = load("arley_charts", ROOT / "scripts" / "arley_charts.py")

rate = acharts.rate_chart(
    0.25,
    t_max=20,
    y_max=5,
    legend_font_size=21,
    annotation_font_size=20,
    t_ticks=[0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20],
    rate_ticks=[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
    width=960,
    height=290,
)
display(
    rate.configure(font="Libertinus Serif", background="#FAFAFA")
    .configure_axis(labelFontSize=22, titleFontSize=26)
    .configure_legend(symbolSize=200)
)
display(Markdown("Subcritical after $t = 4$: $\\mu(t) > \\lambda$."))
```

## Random draws per tree grow with time

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{python}
import numpy as np

adraws = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "benchmarks" / "data" / "draws.csv")
adraws = adraws[
    (adraws["model"] == "arley")
    & (adraws["cell_set"] == "grid")
    & np.isclose(adraws["slope"], 0.25)
]
adraw_all = acharts.curves_from_draws(adraws)  # every T, used by the log-axis graph
adraws = adraws[adraws["T"] <= 20]
adraw_curves = acharts.curves_from_draws(adraws)

adraw_chart = acharts.draws_chart(
    adraw_curves,
    alt.X(
        "T:Q",
        scale=alt.Scale(domain=[1, 20], nice=False),
        title="terminal time T",
        axis=alt.Axis(values=[1, 5, 10, 15, 20], format="d"),
    ),
    legend_font_size=21,
    width=960,
    height=265,
)
display(
    adraw_chart.configure(font="Libertinus Serif", background="#FAFAFA")
    .configure_axis(labelFontSize=22, titleFontSize=26)
    .configure_legend(symbolSize=200)
)

adraw_mean = adraw_curves[adraw_curves["T"] == adraw_curves["T"].max()].set_index(
    "method"
)["mean"]
adraw_ratio = adraw_mean[acharts.LABEL_RUN] / adraw_mean[acharts.LABEL_CONTOUR]
display(
    Markdown(
        f"At $T = {adraw_curves['T'].max():g}$, splitting draws "
        f"**{adraw_ratio:,.0f}×** more random numbers.\n\n"
        f'[$\\lambda = 1$, $\\mu(t) = t/4$]{{style="{PARAM_STYLE}"}}'
    )
)
```
:::
